short_definition: Pay yourself first is a money habit where you automatically move a set amount to savings or investments as soon as you're paid, before spending on anything else.
explanation: To pay yourself first, pick a fixed amount or percentage of each paycheck to save or invest. Then automate it on payday with a scheduled bank transfer, a split direct deposit or a workplace retirement contribution. You budget and spend only what remains.

This makes saving the default. You no longer rely on whatever is left at the end of the month, which is often nothing. Automation also removes a recurring decision, so building an emergency fund or long-term savings becomes more consistent.

The main risk is setting the amount too high. You could run short for essential bills and end up paying overdraft fees or credit card interest that costs more than your savings earn. Cover essentials and minimum debt payments first, start with a manageable amount and raise it over time. If you have high-interest debt, weigh paying it down against saving.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): You earn $2,500 a month after tax. On payday, an automatic transfer moves 10% ($250) to a high-yield savings account, and you budget the remaining $2,250 for bills and spending. After 12 months you have saved $3,000 before interest, without deciding to save each month.
common_mistake: Setting the automatic transfer so high that you have to move money back or lean on a credit card later in the month. Start with an amount you can sustain and raise it gradually.
title: Pay Yourself First
